R05-D-01: Every wave of labour-saving machinery revives an old piece of arithmetic. If a factory needs a fixed quantity of work done, and a new machine does a third of it, then a third of the workers must go. Extend the sum across a whole economy and the conclusion seems inescapable: the more productive we become, the fewer of us will be needed. Economists have a name for the premise hidden in this calculation. They call it the lump of labour fallacy, the assumption that there is a set amount of work to be shared out, so that any work done by a machine, a newcomer or a pensioner who stays on is necessarily work taken from someone else. The premise fails because the quantity of work is not fixed; it depends on what people want and can afford. When a machine makes cloth cheaper, households that once owned two shirts buy five, and the money they no longer spend on clothing goes on furniture, travel or schooling, each of which employs someone. The jobs created in this way are rarely the jobs that were lost, and they often appear in places and trades that nobody at the time thought to connect with the original invention. That is precisely why the destruction is so visible and the creation so easy to overlook. A closed mill is a single event with an address; the thousand small expansions that follow are scattered across an economy and are reported, if at all, as ordinary growth. The same error appears in proposals that look generous. Schemes to push older workers into early retirement so that the young can find work, or to cap weekly hours so that employment is spread more thinly, assume that the jobs given up by one group pass intact to another. There is little reason to expect this. A worker who retires early also stops earning and spending at the old rate, and a firm that loses an experienced employee may simply produce less rather than hire a novice to take her place. None of this means that the anxiety is foolish. The fallacy concerns the total amount of work, not its distribution, and a correct argument about totals is cold comfort to a fifty-year-old weaver whose skills no longer have a buyer. Transitions can take a generation, and the people who bear their cost are seldom the people who collect the gains. The proper conclusion is narrower than either side usually admits: technology does not abolish work in aggregate, but it can ruin particular lives and places, and policy ought to be judged by what it does for them rather than by whether it rescues a fixed stock of jobs that never existed.
R05-D-02: Labour law in most countries rests on a binary. A worker is either an employee, who accepts direction in exchange for a wage and a bundle of protections, or an independent contractor, who sells a result, chooses her own methods and bears her own risks. The line was drawn for a world in which the difference was usually obvious: the clerk at a desk was one, the plumber who came to fix the office pipes was the other. Platform work has made the line hard to find. A driver who logs into an app chooses when to work and may refuse any job, which looks like independence; the same driver cannot set the fare, does not know which passenger comes next, and can be removed by an algorithm whose criteria she never sees, which looks very much like direction. Two responses dominate the debate. One holds that platform workers are employees in all but name and that courts should simply say so. The other holds that flexibility is the whole attraction of such work, that many who do it also study or hold other jobs, and that imposing fixed shifts, minimum hours and the rest of the employment bundle would destroy the thing they value. Each side is right about what the other ignores. The first is right that the platform exercises a control over the terms of work that no genuine contractor would accept; the second is right that the employment bundle was designed around a fixed schedule and a single employer, and fits awkwardly onto someone who works eleven hours one week for three different apps and none the next. What both share is the assumption that protections must come as a package attached to a status. That assumption is a historical accident rather than a principle. Some protections, such as a minimum rate for time actually worked, insurance against injury on the job or a right to be told why an account was suspended, depend on nothing that a flexible schedule makes impossible. Others, such as paid holidays calculated over a working year, are harder to translate, though not obviously impossible if entitlements accrue by the hour and follow the worker rather than the firm. Unbundling has dangers of its own. A menu of separable protections invites firms to lobby for the cheapest selection, and a third category of worker, introduced to accommodate the platforms, could become a convenient place to move people who are at present employees. The case for unbundling is therefore not that it is free of risk, but that the binary has already failed: forcing a new form of work into one of two old boxes guarantees that, whichever box is chosen, a large part of the reality will be misdescribed.
R05-D-03: Why does a string quartet cost so much more to hear today, relative to a shirt or a radio, than it did a century ago? Not because the musicians have become greedy or the concert halls inefficient. Performing a quartet required four players and roughly forty minutes then, and it requires the same now; no innovation has allowed three musicians to play it in half the time without destroying the thing being bought. Meanwhile workers in manufacturing have become many times more productive, and their wages have risen accordingly. The musicians' pay must rise too, or they would drift into other work. So the price of the quartet climbs relative to goods whose production has been transformed, even though nothing about the quartet has changed. Economists sometimes call this the cost disease, and its reach goes far beyond concert halls. Teaching, nursing, care of the elderly and much legal and administrative work share the quartet's structure: the service largely consists of a person's time and attention, and attempts to compress that time often degrade what is delivered. A class of sixty is cheaper per pupil than a class of thirty, but it is not the same product at a lower price. Where productivity in such sectors lags, their share of national spending rises, and with it a persistent suspicion that schools and hospitals are squandering money, since nearly everything else seems to be getting cheaper. The diagnosis contains a consolation that is often missed. If the relative cost of services rises because the rest of the economy has become more productive, then society as a whole is richer, and can afford those services even at their higher relative price. A family that spends a larger share of its income on its children's schooling than its grandparents did may also own far more and work fewer hours. What feels like a crisis of affordability is, on this view, partly a change in the composition of a growing budget. The argument should not be stretched into a blanket excuse. That some cost growth in services is unavoidable does not mean that all of it is; administrative layers can multiply in a hospital as easily as in any other organisation, and the cost disease offers them no defence. Nor is the consolation automatic. The higher relative price of care falls hardest on those whose incomes have not shared in the general gain, and public budgets that depend on taxes voters resist may cut services long before the arithmetic says they must. The cost disease explains a pattern; it does not settle who should pay for it.
R05-D-04: Arguments about working from home usually turn on a single question: are people as productive at the kitchen table as they are at the office desk? For many experienced professionals the honest answer appears to be yes, or close enough. They know their jobs, they know whom to ask, and they gain hours that once disappeared into commuting. But the question is framed around the output of a worker who is already competent, and it says little about how anyone becomes competent in the first place. Consider a hypothetical accounting firm that sends everyone home. Its partners notice no fall in billable work during the first year, and the move looks like a clear success. What they cannot see is what their newest recruits are missing. In an office, a junior accountant overhears a senior colleague talking a nervous client through a bad result, watches how a disputed figure is checked, and asks a quick question that would feel too trivial to put in an email. None of this appears in any measure of output, and almost none of it is deliberately taught. It is absorbed, in the way apprentices have always absorbed a trade, by being near people who practise it. Remote arrangements tend to remove exactly this kind of learning, because it depends on unplanned exposure and remote work is organised around planned contact. A video call is scheduled, has an agenda and ends when the agenda is done. The junior who would have learnt by watching instead learns only what someone remembered to explain. The cost is real but delayed: it shows up years later, as a cohort of mid-career staff who are slower to exercise judgement than their predecessors were at the same stage, by which time the decision that caused it has long been forgotten. This is not an argument for ordering everyone back to their desks. Offices have never guaranteed this kind of learning; a junior placed among seniors who keep their doors shut learns little more than one at home. Firms can also try to replace accidental exposure with deliberate arrangements, such as pairing juniors with seniors on live work or inviting them to sit in on difficult calls. The point is that such arrangements must be built on purpose, and a firm that judges remote work only by the output of its experienced staff will not notice that it needs them until the damage is done.
R05-D-05: Early researchers in artificial intelligence made a natural assumption about which problems would yield first. They took easy to mean what people find easy and hard to mean what people find hard, and so they assumed that a machine which could play respectable chess or prove theorems in logic would soon be able to fold laundry or cross a cluttered room. Matters turned out almost the other way round. Programs that could beat strong players at board games arrived long before machines that could reliably pick up an unfamiliar object without crushing or dropping it. The observation that the faculties we think of as higher are the cheap ones to mechanise, while those we take for granted are expensive, has come to be described by roboticists as a paradox. It is a paradox only if our sense of difficulty is a good guide to the difficulty of a task, and a plausible explanation is that it is not. Perception and movement have been refined over an immense evolutionary history, and they run beneath awareness, so they feel like nothing at all. Explicit reasoning is recent and effortful, and its effortfulness is precisely what we notice. The feeling of difficulty, on this account, measures how new a skill is to our species rather than how much computation it requires. The implication for work is uncomfortable for a familiar way of ranking jobs. We tend to treat the skills of the hospital cleaner, the gardener and the care worker as basic and those of the clerk who reconciles accounts as advanced. Yet the cleaner moves through rooms that are never arranged twice in the same way and handles objects of every shape and texture, while the reconciliation follows rules that can be written down. A machine finds the second job far easier to take over than the first. Forecasts that expect automation to climb steadily upward from the bottom of the wage scale may therefore have the direction partly backwards. Two cautions are in order. First, the paradox describes a stage of technology, not a law of nature; methods that learn from vast numbers of examples have already eroded some of the advantage that perception once enjoyed, and it would be rash to assume the boundary will stay where it is. Second, being hard to automate is not the same as being well rewarded. The skills that resist machines are often widely shared among people, and abundance keeps wages low whatever a robot can or cannot do. The paradox tells us which tasks machines will struggle with; it does not tell us that the people who perform them will prosper.
R05-D-06: The economist's textbook treats a trade union as a cartel of sellers. By bargaining collectively, workers withhold their labour unless paid more than a competitive market would offer, and the familiar consequences follow: fewer people employed in the unionised firm, more crowding into the sectors that remain open, and an output somewhat smaller than it might have been. On this view the only interesting question about a union is how large a premium it extracts and how much inefficiency that premium causes. Whatever else unions do, their grievance committees, their disputes over safety rules, their elected stewards on the shop floor, is incidental to the price they set. That picture leaves out a choice every dissatisfied worker faces. She can leave, taking her skills to another employer, or she can stay and try to change what troubles her. Without a union, leaving is often the only safe course, because an individual who complains about a dangerous machine or an arbitrary supervisor marks herself as troublesome, and whatever she might have told the firm is lost when she walks out. A union changes the calculation. It allows complaints to be made collectively, through procedures, by people who cannot easily be singled out, and so it converts a stream of quiet departures into a stream of information that management would otherwise have had to buy, if it could buy it at all. Firms that hear this information may lose fewer trained workers and correct faults they did not know they had. Seen this way, a union has two faces, and the question is not which of them is real but which predominates in a given setting. Where management treats the grievance procedure as an adversary to be outmanoeuvred, voice tends to harden into obstruction, and the cartel face is what remains. Where management treats the same procedure as an early warning, voice can make the firm more productive than a non-union rival, enough in some cases to offset the higher wage bill. The evidence on unions and productivity is accordingly mixed, and it ought to be; a single average effect conceals the very variation that matters. This is why measuring unions only by their wage premium is a category error rather than a harmless simplification. It judges an institution that partly exists to carry information by the one effect, the price it sets, that carries no information about what is going wrong on the shop floor. It also hides the fact that the value of voice depends on whether anyone is listening, so that the same union under a different management can be a burden or an asset. None of this establishes that unions are good for firms, still less that they always raise productivity. It establishes only that the question cannot be answered by looking at the price of labour alone.
R05-D-07: For about a century after industrialisation, the working week in the richer economies shrank steadily, from something like sixty hours or more to around forty. Many observers assumed the trend would continue. If each generation could produce more in an hour than the last, it seemed natural that part of the gain would be taken as leisure, and confident predictions were made in the early twentieth century that the grandchildren of that era might work perhaps fifteen hours a week. In much of the rich world the decline instead slowed sharply after the middle of the century, and for many full-time professionals it appears to have reversed. The puzzle is not that people work at all, but that productivity kept rising while the hours of so many stopped falling. The simplest explanation is that people chose income over time. Higher pay makes an hour of leisure more expensive, since each hour off now forgoes more, and it also makes people richer, so that they can afford more leisure. Which of these pulls is stronger is an empirical matter, and for a long period the second seemed to win. Perhaps, the argument runs, it simply stopped winning: people discovered new things to want faster than their incomes satisfied the old wants. A related account adds that much of what people buy matters to them chiefly in relation to what others have, so that a general rise in income buys no one a better position and the race to earn resumes at a higher level. Both accounts treat hours as something workers choose, as they might choose how much bread to buy. That premise deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. For most employees hours come attached to a job, and the menu of jobs is set largely by employers. A firm that pays a fixed cost for each person it hires, in recruitment, training, benefits and supervision, has good reason to prefer fewer people working longer to more people working less. In many professions, moreover, long hours have become a signal of commitment, and promotion goes to those who send it; a lawyer who would gladly trade a fifth of her salary for a fifth of her week may find that the trade is not on offer at all, or that it costs her far more than a fifth of her career. Under such conditions the hours we observe tell us what jobs offer, not what workers want. The institutional account has a limitation of its own. It cannot easily explain why some people, given a genuine choice, still work very long hours, and it would be a mistake to deny that for many of them the work itself is the attraction. Nor are the averages uniform. In some economies the same decades that lengthened the week for well-paid professionals left many lower-paid workers with fewer hours than they wanted, pieced together from part-time or irregular shifts. An average that holds steady can conceal one group working too much and another too little. What follows is that the old prediction failed less because of a mistake about human desire than because of a mistake about how labour markets work. The forecasters assumed that rising productivity would be divided between income and leisure by the free choices of workers. The division has in fact been made largely by the structure of jobs, and that structure can be altered: by rules on hours, by the way benefits are financed, by what firms choose to reward. Whether people would then work less is an open question, but it is one that the present arrangement prevents us from answering.
R05-D-08: For a long time the standard story about technology and pay was a story about skill. New machines, and computers above all, were thought to complement educated workers and to substitute for the rest, so that demand for the educated rose faster than their supply and the gap between their wages and everyone else's widened. Inequality, in this account, was the outcome of a contest in which schooling had to keep pace with machines, and the remedy was plain: produce more graduates. The story had the virtue of simplicity and the defect of predicting a smooth gradient, with the prospects of jobs improving in proportion to the schooling they required. What many studies of rich economies in the closing decades of the twentieth century found instead was a hollowing out. Employment grew at the top of the wage distribution and, more surprisingly, at the bottom, while the middle shrank. The explanation that has largely displaced the skill story looks not at workers but at tasks. A computer, on this view, is good at carrying out any procedure that can be fully specified in advance, and the jobs made up mostly of such procedures, keeping ledgers, typing correspondence, inspecting items on a production line, happened to sit in the middle of the wage scale. Jobs at the top require judgement and the framing of problems; many jobs at the bottom, guarding a building, preparing food, helping an elderly person to bathe, require adaptability in physical settings that no program could specify. Neither kind of task was routine, and so both survived. The task view is a real advance. It explains a pattern the skill view could not, and it shifts attention from the credentials of workers to the content of work. But its central category is less solid than it appears. Whether a task counts as routine is usually settled by asking whether it has in fact been automated, and a classification fixed by results cannot then be used to predict them without circularity. Tasks once thought to demand judgement, such as reading medical images or drafting standard contracts, are now discussed as candidates for automation, and if they are automated they will be relabelled routine after the event. The line between routine and non-routine describes the frontier of a particular technology; it is not a fact about the tasks themselves. A second difficulty is subtler. Both the skill story and the task story treat technology as an external force that arrives and to which labour markets adjust. Yet which tasks are automated is a decision made by firms, and it depends on what machines cost relative to people, on how the tax system treats investment in equipment compared with spending on wages, and on whether managers regard workers as a cost to be reduced or a capacity to be developed. The same software can be deployed to remove a clerk or to let her handle cases that once needed a specialist. Polarisation, from this angle, is not simply what computers do to jobs; it is partly what a given set of incentives led firms to do with computers. None of this makes the task view wrong, and it would be careless to replace one tidy determinism with another in which every outcome is a choice. Some tasks really are cheaper to mechanise than others, and no tax code will make a typing pool competitive again. The claim is narrower: that the shape of the wage distribution reflects technology filtered through institutions, and that a theory which treats the filter as fixed will mistake a policy question for a law of nature.
